summaries.summary: Twitter faces widespread online harassment, especially toward women, making automated sexual harassment content detection important for reducing human effort and flagging or removing content.
Previous studies addressed sexism and racism broadly or used benevolent and hostile sexism, with little focus on different online harassment types using natural language processing.
This work for the SociaL Media And Harassment Competition of the ECML PKDD 2019 Conference uses competition tweet data and RNNs with deep, classification-specific attention.

Prior work categorized hateful tweets as sexist, racist or neither, then developed hostile and benevolent sexism and broader harassment categories including indirect harassment, information threat, sexual harassment and physical harassment.

Related hate speech detection approaches include SVMs, RNNs, FastText, SemEval2018 evaluations, text augmentation, convolutional and gated recurrent networks, attention mechanisms, two-step classification and RNN ensembles.
The Twitter dataset has train, validation and test sets, harassment and non-harassment categories, three harassment sub-categories, and imbalance affecting results.
Back-translation of indirect and physical harassment train tweets from english to german, french and greek and back to english augments data and boosts model performance.
Pre-trained word embeddings from 2B Twitter data having 27B tokens initialize the embedding layer.
A tweet pre-processor cleans and tokenizes the dataset before model training.
The attention-based approach uses RNN models with GRU cells to transform tweet tokens into hidden states, followed by an LR Layer for classification.
The paragraph defines the proposed hidden state, reset gate, update gate, sigmoid function, matrices, biases, and the LR Layer probability estimate.
An attention mechanism similar to BIBREF9 is added so the LR Layer considers the weighted sum h_sum of all hidden states instead of h_k.
The weighted sum is defined as h_sum = sum from t=1 to k of alpha_t h_t.
The attention RNN probability is defined as P_attentionRNN = sigma(W_p h_sum + b_p).
Alternatively, h_sum can pass through an MLP with k layers before the LR layer estimates the corresponding probability.
The alternative attention RNN probability is defined as P_attentionRNN = sigma(W_p h_* + b_p).
The classification-specific attention mechanism assigns larger weights to harassment evidence, uses four attention mechanisms, one per category, and adds a projection layer for word embeddings.

The architecture uses dimension 200 Twitter embeddings, Spatial Dropout, a one-layer MLP with tanh and 128 hidden units, a unidirectional GRU with 1 Stacked Layer and size 128, four self-attentions, and a one-layer MLP with 128 nodes and ReLU.
This subsection gives training process details and describes the different models compared in the experiments.
Training uses batch size 32, epochs = 20, patience = 10, and average AUC as early stopping criterion because the dataset is imbalanced.
Training optimizes the loss function with the Adam optimizer BIBREF20 and learning rate equal to 0.001.
The loss function is L = 1/2 BCE(harassment) + 1/2(1/5 BCE(sexualH) + 2/5 BCE(indirectH) + 2/5 BCE(physicalH)).
BCE is the binary cross-entropy loss function.
BCE is defined as -1/n sum from i=1 to n of [y_i log(y'_i) + (1 - y_i) log(1 - y'_i)].
The loss function weights both tasks equally and gives higher weight in the second task to categories harder to predict due to class imbalance.
Each model produces four scores, and a threshold equal to 0.33 determines harassment labels and the harassment type with the greatest score.
Eight models are compared, differing by Projected Layer presence, including LastStateRNN, AvgRNN, AttentionRNN and MultiAttentionRNN with four attentions.
Models were evaluated using F1 Score over ten runs, with multi-attention models outperforming others and the Projected Layer version achieving the highest F1 Macro.
The attention-based RNN approach detects harassment language and harassment types, with the multi-attention method having a projected layer achieving the highest F1 Score performance.
Future work will perform more experiments with this dataset applying different models using BERT BIBREF21 and apply the presented models to other hate speech datasets.
